subject: math
domain: Statistics and Probability — Making Inferences and Justifying Conclusions
cluster: Make inferences and justify conclusions from sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies
intro: When you cannot measure a whole population, you take a random sample and use a single sample value, a point estimate, to stand in for the unknown population value, the parameter. For a quantitative variable the sample mean $\bar{x}$ estimates the population mean $\mu$; for a categorical variable the sample proportion $\hat{p}=\dfrac{x}{n}$ estimates the population proportion $p$. Because a different random sample would give a slightly different estimate, you attach a margin of error. You can read it off a simulation as the half-width of the middle $95\%$ of resampled estimates, or compute it by formula as $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE$, where $SE_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$ and $SE_{\bar{x}}=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$. Reporting $\text{estimate}\pm\text{ME}$ gives a $95\%$ confidence interval, and the margin of error shrinks like $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ as the sample grows.

items.prompt: In a random sample of $200$ registered voters, $116$ say they support a new transit measure. Use the sample to estimate the proportion of all voters in the city who support the measure.

steps: The unknown population proportion $p$ is the parameter. The best point estimate from the sample is the sample proportion $\hat{p}$.
Compute $\hat{p}=\dfrac{x}{n}=\dfrac{116}{200}$.
So we estimate that about $58\%$ of all city voters support the measure.

items.prompt: A random sample of $5$ morning commute times (in minutes) is $22,\ 18,\ 25,\ 30,\ 20$. Estimate the mean commute time $\mu$ for the whole population of commuters.

steps: The population mean $\mu$ is the parameter; the sample mean $\bar{x}$ is the point estimate.
Divide by the sample size $n=5$: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{115}{5}$.
Simplify: $\dfrac{115}{5}=23$.
So we estimate the population mean commute time is $\bar{x}=23$ minutes.

items.prompt: To gauge the spread of the estimate in Example 1, a computer resamples $n=50$ voters many times. The middle $95\%$ of the simulated sample proportions run from $0.46$ to $0.62$, centered at $0.54$. Find the margin of error and write the $95\%$ interval estimate.

steps: The margin of error is the half-width of the middle $95\%$ of the simulated estimates, not the full width.
Width of the middle $95\%$: $0.62-0.46=0.16$.
Half-width: $\text{ME}=\dfrac{0.16}{2}=0.08$.
Attach it to the center estimate: $0.54\pm 0.08$.
The endpoints are $0.54-0.08=0.46$ and $0.54+0.08=0.62$, so the $95\%$ interval runs from $0.46$ to $0.62$.

items.prompt: Using the data from Example 1, where $\hat{p}=0.58$ from a sample of $n=200$, compute the standard error, find the $95\%$ margin of error with $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE$, and state the $95\%$ confidence interval for the true proportion of supporters.

steps: Standard error of a proportion: $SE_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$.
Take the square root: $SE\approx 0.0349$.
Margin of error for $95\%$ confidence: $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE=2(0.0349)\approx 0.070$.
Build the interval: $\hat{p}\pm\text{ME}=0.58\pm 0.07$, giving endpoints $0.58-0.07=0.51$ and $0.58+0.07=0.65$.
Interpretation: we are $95\%$ confident that the true proportion of all voters who support the measure lies between $0.51$ and $0.65$ (that is, between $51\%$ and $65\%$).
solution.answer: $SE\approx 0.035$, $\text{ME}\approx 0.07$, and the $95\%$ interval is $0.58\pm 0.07$, i.e. $0.51$ to $0.65$

items.prompt: A polling firm finds that a sample of $n=400$ voters gives a margin of error of $0.05$ for an estimated proportion. The firm wants to cut the margin of error in half to $0.025$ for the next poll. How large must the new sample size be, and why?

steps: The margin of error is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, so $\text{ME}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$.
Because $\sqrt{n}$ is in the denominator, halving $\text{ME}$ requires doubling $\sqrt{n}$.
Doubling $\sqrt{n}$ means multiplying $n$ itself by $2^2=4$, since $(2\sqrt{n})^2=4n$.
Multiply the original sample size by $4$: $n=4\times 400=1600$.

Check: $\sqrt{1600}=40$ is twice $\sqrt{400}=20$, so the margin of error is halved to $0.025$. Doubling $n$ alone would only shrink $\text{ME}$ by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\approx 0.71$, not in half.
solution.answer: $n=1600$; quadrupling the sample size halves the margin of error because $\text{ME}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$

items.prompt: In a random sample of $150$ smartphone owners, $54$ say they upgrade their phone every year. Estimate the proportion $p$ of all owners who upgrade every year.
items.hint: The point estimate of a population proportion is $\hat{p}=\dfrac{x}{n}$, where $x$ is the count in the category and $n$ is the sample size.

steps: Use $\hat{p}=\dfrac{x}{n}=\dfrac{54}{150}$.
So we estimate that about $36\%$ of all owners upgrade every year.

items.prompt: A random sample of $6$ backpack weights (in pounds) is $14,\ 11,\ 9,\ 16,\ 12,\ 10$. Estimate the population mean backpack weight $\mu$.
items.hint: The point estimate of $\mu$ is the sample mean $\bar{x}=\dfrac{\sum x_i}{n}$. Add the values, then divide by $n=6$.

steps: Divide by $n=6$: $\bar{x}=\dfrac{72}{6}=12$.
So we estimate the population mean backpack weight is $12$ pounds.

items.prompt: A simulation resamples $n=80$ households many times to estimate the proportion who recycle. The middle $95\%$ of the simulated proportions run from $0.61$ to $0.79$, centered at $0.70$. Find the margin of error and write the $95\%$ interval estimate.
items.hint: The margin of error is the half-width of the middle $95\%$, so subtract the endpoints and divide by $2$. Then write $\text{center}\pm\text{ME}$.

steps: Find the width of the middle $95\%$: $0.79-0.61=0.18$.
Halve it for the margin of error: $\text{ME}=\dfrac{0.18}{2}=0.09$.
Attach to the center: $0.70\pm 0.09$.
The endpoints are $0.70-0.09=0.61$ and $0.70+0.09=0.79$, so the $95\%$ interval runs from $0.61$ to $0.79$.

items.prompt: A random sample of $n=64$ boxes has mean weight $\bar{x}=23$ ounces and sample standard deviation $s=8$ ounces. Compute the standard error of the mean, find the $95\%$ margin of error with $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE$, and state the $95\%$ interval estimate for $\mu$.
items.hint: Use $SE_{\bar{x}}=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ with $\sqrt{n}$ in the denominator, not $n$. Then $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE$ and the interval is $\bar{x}\pm\text{ME}$.

steps: Standard error of a mean: $SE_{\bar{x}}=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{64}}$.
Since $\sqrt{64}=8$, $SE=\dfrac{8}{8}=1$ ounce.
Margin of error: $\text{ME}\approx 2\cdot SE=2(1)=2$ ounces.
Interval: $\bar{x}\pm\text{ME}=23\pm 2$, with endpoints $21$ and $25$.
We are $95\%$ confident the true mean box weight $\mu$ lies between $21$ and $25$ ounces.
solution.answer: $SE=1$, $\text{ME}=2$, and the $95\%$ interval is $23\pm 2$ ounces, i.e. $21$ to $25$ ounces

items.prompt: A survey of $n=900$ adults gives an estimated proportion with a margin of error of $0.04$. A researcher claims that to shrink the margin of error to $0.02$, it is enough to double the sample size to $1800$. Is the claim correct? If not, find the sample size actually needed.
items.hint: Because $\text{ME}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, halving the margin of error requires multiplying $n$ by $4$, not $2$. Compare what doubling $n$ actually does.

steps: The margin of error is proportional to $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, so to halve $\text{ME}$ you must double $\sqrt{n}$, which means multiplying $n$ by $4$.
Needed sample size: $n=4\times 900=3600$.

Check the claim: doubling $n$ to $1800$ multiplies $\sqrt{n}$ by only $\sqrt{2}$, so $\text{ME}$ shrinks by a factor of $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\approx 0.71$, giving about $0.04\times 0.71\approx 0.028$, not $0.02$.
So the claim is wrong: doubling $n$ is not enough. The researcher needs $n=3600$ to reach a margin of error of $0.02$.
solution.answer: The claim is incorrect; a sample of $n=3600$ is needed because $\text{ME}\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$ (quadrupling $n$ halves $\text{ME}$)
